title: Digital Financial Services and Sustainable Development: Temporal Trade-Offs and the Moderating Role of Financial Literacy
tldr: Examines how mobile financial services usage affects short-term and long-term financial behaviors differently, with financial literacy dimensions moderating these effects, using data from 21,757 U.S. adults.
problem_and_motivation: Mobile financial services may simultaneously improve long-term planning and undermine short-term financial discipline, but no study has empirically tested these dual temporal effects or how financial literacy dimensions differentially moderate them.
approach: Analyzed data from 21,757 U.S. adults in the 2021 National Financial Capability Study using structural equation modeling.
Drew on Construal Level Theory, Dual Process Theory, and Social Cognitive Theory as the theoretical framework.
Measured financial literacy across three dimensions: objective knowledge (OK), subjective knowledge (SK), and perceived ability (PA).
Modeled both short-term financial behaviors (spending control, emergency preparedness) and long-term behaviors (retirement planning, investment).
Examined MFS effects through the lens of Sustainable Development Goals 1, 8, and 10.
findings: num: MFS usage negatively affects short-term behaviors (spending control and emergency preparedness).
num: MFS usage positively influences long-term behaviors (retirement planning and investment participation).
Objective knowledge (OK) provides protective benefits against MFS-induced short-term risks.
Perceived ability (PA) paradoxically exacerbates adverse short-term effects of MFS usage.
Subjective knowledge (SK) shows different moderating patterns from OK and PA.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides the first large-scale empirical test of the dual temporal effects of MFS on financial behavior, confirming that digital convenience simultaneously undermines short-term discipline and enhances long-term planning. It demonstrates that financial literacy dimensions have differential moderating effects, with objective knowledge protecting against short-term risks while perceived ability can exacerbate them. The study connects individual financial behaviors to systemic sustainable development outcomes.
directly_justifies: MFS usage has opposing effects on short-term vs. long-term financial behaviors.
Objective financial knowledge protects against MFS-related short-term spending risks.
Perceived financial ability may paradoxically increase risky behavior in digital environments.
limits: U.S.-specific sample may not generalize to Philippine or other developing-country contexts.
Cross-sectional design limits causal inference about MFS effects on behavior.
Self-reported financial behaviors may differ from actual transaction data.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematic scan across all 14 topic domains was performed. Domain 1 (Financial Behavior) was flagged as medium relevance because the paper examines digital financial behavior patterns. Domain 2 (Financial Preferences) was flagged as medium because user-declared financial literacy moderates behavior. Domain 5 (Profiles) was flagged as medium because differential effects across literacy dimensions imply behavioral profiles. All other domains were rejected: the paper does not address expense categorization, predictive modeling, budgeting algorithms, anomaly detection, mobile UX design, or ML serving.

limitations: U.S.-only sample limits cross-cultural applicability, especially to Philippine context. [unacknowledged]
Cross-sectional survey data prevents causal attribution of MFS effects.
Self-report measures may introduce recall and social desirability bias.
remember_this: MFS improves long-term planning but undermines short-term spending control.
Objective knowledge protects against digital overspending; perceived ability can worsen it.
Study of 21,757 U.S. adults reveals systematic temporal trade-offs in digital finance.
Digital-specific financial literacy programs should emphasize realistic risk assessment.
